subject: Urology
title: Bladder Cancer
subtitle: Epidemiology, pathology, staging, clinical picture, investigations, treatment and urinary diversion
sourceNote: Built only from the uploaded Bladder Cancer lecture by Dr Amr Hassan Alkhalily. The bank preserves the lecture terminology, figures, percentages, staging statements and treatment pathways without adding external guideline updates. Legible handwritten teaching annotations were included only when unambiguous.

cases.title: Older Smoker with Painless Visible Haematuria
cases.scenario: An older smoker presents with visible painless haematuria. Examination is unremarkable.
cases.ar: مريض كبير ومدخن عنده painless visible haematuria والفحص طبيعي.
questions: What is the most important suspected diagnosis?
State the two most important risk factors in the lecture.
What is the primary diagnostic modality?
answer: Urine analysis, urine cytology, imaging with ultrasound/CT/MRI, and cystoscopy with biopsy.
cases.trap: Early bladder cancer may have an unremarkable examination.
cases.memory: Painless haematuria in an older smoker = bladder cancer until proven otherwise.

cases.title: Bilharzial Patient with Bladder Tumour
cases.scenario: A patient with a history of schistosomiasis develops a bladder malignancy.
cases.ar: مريض عنده bilharziasis وظهر له bladder tumour.
questions: Which histological subtype is specifically associated with schistosomiasis?
List the major bladder cancer histological subtypes.
Which subtype is the commonest overall and what percentage does it represent?
answer: Transitional cell carcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma and sarcoma.
Transitional cell carcinoma, about 80–90% of cases.
cases.trap: Schistosomiasis is linked to SCC, while TCC remains the commonest overall.

cases.title: Papillary Tumour Confined to Urothelium
cases.scenario: Cystoscopy reveals a papillary bladder tumour that has not invaded beneath the urothelium.
questions: How does it differ from Tis and T1?
answer: Tis is carcinoma in situ; T1 invades the subepithelial connective tissue (lamina propria).
cases.trap: Ta is papillary and non-invasive; Tis is flat carcinoma in situ.
cases.memory: Ta = papillary top; Tis = flat in situ; T1 = lamina propria.

cases.title: Flat High-Risk Non-Invasive Lesion
cases.scenario: A flat bladder lesion is diagnosed as carcinoma in situ.
cases.ar: Flat lesion واتشخص carcinoma in situ.
questions: Outline the treatment options stated in the lecture.
answer: TURBT/resection is the mainstay for non-muscle-invasive disease, with intravesical BCG or Mitomycin C for higher-risk disease; radical cystectomy may be offered for high-risk disease or limited response.
cases.trap: Although non-muscle-invasive, carcinoma in situ is treated as higher-risk disease in the lecture.
cases.memory: CIS = Tis, non-invasive but high risk.

cases.title: Tumour Invading Lamina Propria
cases.scenario: Histology shows invasion into subepithelial connective tissue without invasion of muscularis propria.
cases.ar: Tumour داخل الـlamina propria لكن مش داخل muscle.
questions: Classify it as muscle-invasive or non-muscle-invasive.
cases.trap: T1 is invasive into connective tissue but still classified as non-muscle-invasive.
cases.memory: T1 reaches lamina propria, not muscle.

cases.title: Tumour Invading Detrusor Muscle
cases.scenario: A bladder tumour invades the muscular layer of the bladder wall in a surgically fit patient.
cases.ar: Tumour وصل للـdetrusor muscle والمريض fit للجراحة.
questions: What is the standard surgical treatment in the lecture?
What systemic treatment is often considered before surgery?
answer: Radical cystectomy with complete removal of the bladder.
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy, typically a cisplatin combination regimen.
Regular follow-up with CT imaging for local and distant recurrence.
cases.trap: Muscle invasion changes the treatment pathway from TURBT-based management to radical cystectomy-based management.
cases.memory: T2 muscle → neoadjuvant cisplatin + radical cystectomy.

cases.title: Tumour Extending into Perivesical Fat
cases.scenario: A bladder malignancy extends through the muscle into perivesical fat and the patient reports pelvic pain.
cases.ar: Tumour طلع بره العضلة ووصل للدهون حوالين المثانة مع pelvic pain.
questions: How is this disease category described?
What symptom is compatible with locally advanced disease?
cases.trap: T3 means perivesical fat, while T4 means adjacent organs.

cases.title: Ureteric Orifice Obstruction by Bladder Tumour
cases.scenario: A patient with bladder cancer develops obstruction at the ureteric orifice.
cases.ar: Bladder tumour قافل ureteric orifice والمريض عنده renal colic.
questions: What broad work-up is required for haematuria?
List the common differential diagnoses in the lecture.
answer: Features of ureteric obstruction, including renal colic.
A full work-up for potential bladder cancer.
Urinary tract infection, renal calculi, prostate cancer and renal cancer.
cases.trap: Renal colic here may be caused by tumour obstruction, not only a stone.
cases.memory: Tumour at ureteric orifice → obstruction → renal colic.

cases.title: Recurrent Non-Muscle-Invasive Tumour
cases.scenario: A patient treated for a non-muscle-invasive bladder tumour returns for surveillance because of the high recurrence rate.
cases.ar: مريض اتعالج من NMIBC وراجع متابعة عشان نسبة الرجوع عالية.
questions: What recurrence figure is stated in the lecture?
answer: Regular surveillance with urine cytology and cystoscopy.
cases.trap: The lecture stresses both high recurrence and the possibility that recurrence becomes more invasive.

cases.title: High-Risk NMIBC with Limited Response
cases.scenario: A patient with high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer has a limited response to TURBT and intravesical treatment.
cases.ar: High-risk NMIBC ما استجابش كويس لـTURBT والintravesical therapy.
questions: Where can intravesical therapy be administered?
What definitive surgery may be offered?
cases.trap: Radical cystectomy is not restricted to muscle-invasive disease; the lecture also offers it for high-risk or poorly responding NMIBC.
cases.memory: High-risk/poor response NMIBC may need cystectomy.

cases.title: Post-Cystectomy Patient Requiring Diversion
cases.scenario: After radical cystectomy, a patient requires a method of urinary diversion.
cases.ar: بعد radical cystectomy لازم نختار urinary diversion.
questions: Classify urinary diversion into its two main groups.
answer: Orthotopic bladder substitution, continent reservoir for CIC, and ureterosigmoidostomy.
cases.trap: Do not mix ileal conduit with continent reservoir; ileal conduit is non-continent.

cases.title: Bladder Mass on Ultrasound and CT
cases.scenario: Ultrasound shows a soft-tissue bladder mass with internal vascularity, inseparable from the bladder wall. CT demonstrates focal wall thickening protruding into the lumen.
cases.ar: US فيه vascular mass ملتصقة بالجدار وCT فيه focal wall thickening داخل lumen.
questions: What ultrasound features support bladder cancer?
Which modality is called the primary imaging modality?
Why may MRI be more accurate?
answer: A soft-tissue mass with internal vascularity on colour Doppler that is inseparable from the wall.
Focal bladder-wall thickening or a lesion protruding into the lumen.
MRI more clearly differentiates the bladder-wall layers and uses no ionising radiation.
cases.trap: Cystoscopy remains the primary diagnostic modality even though CT is the primary imaging modality.
cases.memory: CT = primary imaging; cystoscopy = primary diagnosis.

imageQuestions.title: Bladder Wall Diagram
answer: Urothelium is the inner transitional epithelium.
Lamina propria is the subepithelial connective tissue.
Muscularis propria is the detrusor muscle layer.
The outer layer is fatty connective tissue.

a: Non-muscle-invasive disease does not penetrate the deeper muscular layers.
Muscle-invasive disease penetrates the deeper layers/muscularis propria.

detailedShorts.q: Summarise the key conclusions of the lecture.
a: Bladder cancer is frequent and has high mortality.
Key risks include smoking, industrial toxins and bilharzial infestation.
Gross painless haematuria is present in more than 80%.
Cystoscopy is the primary diagnostic modality.
TURBT plus BCG is suitable for non-muscle-invasive disease.

detailedShorts.q: What proportion of patients have gross painless haematuria according to the lecture conclusion?
detailedShorts.a: More than 80%.

detailedShorts.q: Which handwritten features are used to identify higher-risk non-muscle-invasive disease on the treatment slide?
What surveillance interval is written on the non-muscle-invasive bladder-cancer slide?
detailedShorts.a: Every three months.

detailedShorts.q: When is a second-look procedure mentioned in the handwritten non-muscle-invasive treatment annotation?
a: When complete resection was not done.
